lessons.title: Join rows, not circles
lessons.summary: Match keys, preserve unmatched rows, and see why duplicates multiply.

blocks.title: The mental model
blocks.body: A table can contain duplicate keys. Every matching pair contributes a row. Choose INNER, LEFT, FULL, SEMI or ANTI in the visual. The fixture is fully visible; it is not your SQL execution.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.body: A Venn diagram hides row multiplicity. Before summing a joined amount, verify the relationship cardinality.

blocks.title: Before you run
blocks.body: Predict the LEFT JOIN row count. Then compare with INNER, FULL, SEMI and ANTI.

visual.title: Join rows, not circles - visual walkthrough

steps.title: Match keys
steps.body: A join tests pairs of rows. Equal non-null keys match.

steps.title: Preserve rows
steps.body: LEFT keeps unmatched left rows with nulls for the right-hand columns.

steps.title: Count the result
steps.body: Two orders for Ada create two output rows. A join is not set intersection.

steps.title: Null keys
steps.body: With ordinary equality, a null key does not match another null key.

lessons.title: LEFT JOIN: ON versus WHERE
lessons.summary: Keep the customer even when no order satisfies the filter.

blocks.title: The mental model
blocks.body: The same predicate has different consequences in ON and WHERE. Use the visual filter placement control, then edit the SQL file in Try. The Watch fixture does not silently rewrite your file.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.body: WHERE o.status = DONE removes unmatched customers. This does not mean every WHERE predicate turns a LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN; the predicate must reject the null-extended rows.

blocks.title: Before you run
blocks.body: Which customers disappear when the DONE predicate moves into WHERE?

visual.title: LEFT JOIN: ON versus WHERE - visual walkthrough

steps.title: Filter candidate matches
steps.body: A right-side condition in ON restricts which rows can match.

steps.title: Add unmatched rows
steps.body: The LEFT JOIN still preserves customers with no qualifying match.

steps.title: Move it to WHERE
steps.body: WHERE is evaluated after the join. A null right-side status fails status = DONE.

steps.title: Repair the query
steps.body: Move right-side eligibility conditions back into ON when left preservation is required.

lessons.title: GROUP BY and HAVING
lessons.summary: Change the grain deliberately and filter groups after aggregation.

blocks.title: The mental model
blocks.body: Write down what one input row represents and what one output row represents. This query changes the grain from order to customer segment. The real example uses the existing local source.orders seed.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.body: Filtering positive orders before SUM is not the same as filtering groups with a positive net total after SUM.

blocks.title: Before you run
blocks.body: Should a negative order be dropped, or should it reduce the segment total?

code.source:
SELECT segment_id, COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(net_amount) AS revenue
FROM source.orders
GROUP BY segment_id
HAVING SUM(net_amount) > 100
ORDER BY segment_id;

visual.title: GROUP BY and HAVING - visual walkthrough

steps.title: Input grain
steps.body: source.orders contains one row per order.

steps.title: Group
steps.body: Rows with the same segment_id form one group.

steps.title: Aggregate
steps.body: SUM and COUNT reduce each group to one output row.

steps.title: Filter groups
steps.body: HAVING applies to aggregate results; WHERE filters individual input rows.

lessons.title: ROWS, RANGE and peer groups
lessons.summary: Move a window frame and inspect exactly which rows contribute.

blocks.title: The mental model
blocks.body: The visual fixture has two transactions on day 2. ROWS uses the deterministic order (day, txn_id). RANGE uses ORDER BY day, so both peers share the day total. The ordering difference is intentional and displayed.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.body: RANGE is not the same as counting a fixed number of rows. ROWS without a stable tie-breaker can make per-row results nondeterministic.

blocks.title: Before you run
blocks.body: At the first day-2 row, why is ROWS 70 while RANGE is 120?

visual.title: ROWS, RANGE and peer groups - visual walkthrough

steps.title: Keep the rows
steps.body: Unlike GROUP BY, a window adds a value without collapsing the result rows.

steps.title: Order deterministically
steps.body: ROWS uses positions. Include a stable tie-breaker when order matters.

steps.title: Inspect peers
steps.body: RANGE with ORDER BY day includes rows that share the current day.

steps.title: Check the frame
steps.body: The visual compares unbounded preceding to current row. It does not implement arbitrary SQL frames.

lessons.title: Lists, dictionaries and records
lessons.summary: Choose a data structure for lookup instead of repeated nested scans.

blocks.title: The mental model
blocks.body: A dictionary lookup is useful when the key is unique. For one-to-many relationships, build a dictionary of lists or use a table join. The Watch join is an analogy, not execution of this Python.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.body: Replacing a join with a dictionary can silently discard duplicate-key rows.

blocks.title: Before you run
blocks.body: What should happen if two customers share the same id?

code.source:
import pandas as pd
customers = [{"id": 1, "name": "Ada"}, {"id": 2, "name": "Ben"}]
orders = [{"customer_id": 1, "amount": 20}, {"customer_id": 3, "amount": 15}]
by_id = {row["id"]: row["name"] for row in customers}
result = pd.DataFrame([{**o, "name": by_id.get(o["customer_id"])} for o in orders])
result

lessons.title: Broadcast a small dimension
lessons.summary: Separate relational results, join strategy and network movement.

blocks.title: The mental model
blocks.body: SparkLab compiles a bounded PySpark subset into local SQL. Result rows are computed locally; stages, task durations and shuffle volumes are simulated. The Watch buckets are an authored illustration, not Spark telemetry.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.body: No join shuffle does not mean no data movement or no later shuffle. The tiny demo may be auto-broadcast even without the hint; the linked exercise uses authored scale assumptions.

blocks.title: Before you run
blocks.body: Which exchange remains after a broadcast join followed by GROUP BY segment_name?

code.source:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
orders = spark.table("source.orders")
segments = spark.table("source.dim_customer_segment")
joined = orders.join(F.broadcast(segments), "segment_id", "inner")
result = joined.groupBy("segment_name").agg(F.sum("net_amount").alias("revenue"))

lessons.title: Repartition versus coalesce
lessons.summary: See row redistribution, output partitions and the limits of a narrow reduction.

blocks.title: The mental model
blocks.body: The tokens conserve their identities when moving between layouts. Choose the operation and target count. Try uses the existing source.orders table; its runtime plan is separate evidence from the toy visual.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.body: coalesce(1) can concentrate work. A lower shuffle count alone is not proof that a production job will be faster.

blocks.title: Before you run
blocks.body: Pin a run, change coalesce(2) to repartition(2), run again, then compare the recorded plans.

code.source:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
orders = spark.table("source.orders")
result = orders.repartition(8, "customer_id").filter(F.col("net_amount") > 0).coalesce(2)

steps.title: Repartition
steps.body: Reassign rows into new buckets. The visual hash is illustrative, not Spark murmur3.

steps.title: Coalesce
steps.body: Merge existing partitions; asking for more does not increase their number.

steps.title: Read the full plan
steps.body: The example already repartitions once. A final coalesce does not erase that earlier exchange.

lessons.title: Spark windows and ordering
lessons.summary: Reuse the window mental model in the bounded PySpark runtime.

blocks.title: The mental model
blocks.body: The Watch example explains frame semantics. Try runs the seeded orders with actual local result rows and a simulated distributed plan. It is not Apache Spark execution.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.body: The window PARTITION BY is a logical grouping requirement, not a request to create one physical partition per customer.

blocks.title: Before you run
blocks.body: Which columns must stay unchanged for an earlier hash partitioning to be reusable?

code.source:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
from pyspark.sql.window import Window
orders = spark.table("source.orders")
w = Window.partitionBy("customer_id").orderBy("loaded_at", "order_id").rowsBetween(Window.unboundedPreceding, Window.currentRow)
result = orders.withColumn("running_revenue", F.sum("net_amount").over(w))

lessons.title: Declare the grain before joining
lessons.summary: Prevent double counting when combining facts at different levels.

blocks.title: The mental model
blocks.body: Use the input and output grain as a contract. MAX(shipping) works in this tiny example because shipping is constant for each order; it is not a universal fix for duplicate joins.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.body: Joining two fact tables on a non-unique dimension key can multiply both measures.

blocks.title: Before you run
blocks.body: Where should the shipping charge live, and how would you allocate it to products?

code.source:
WITH headers(order_id, shipping) AS (VALUES (1, 10), (2, 6)),
lines(order_id, line_id, amount) AS (VALUES (1, 1, 30), (1, 2, 70), (2, 1, 50))
SELECT h.order_id, COUNT(*) AS lines, SUM(h.shipping) AS duplicated_shipping,
       MAX(h.shipping) AS order_shipping
FROM headers h JOIN lines l ON h.order_id = l.order_id
GROUP BY h.order_id ORDER BY h.order_id;

steps.title: Join

steps.title: Spot fan-out
steps.body: SUM(shipping) now counts the same order cost repeatedly.

steps.body: Aggregate at order grain or allocate shipping using an explicit rule.

lessons.title: History with SCD type 2
lessons.summary: Match an event to the dimension version valid at event time.

blocks.title: The mental model
blocks.body: Business identity and version identity are different. A fact must link to the intended version, not merely the current city.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.body: BETWEEN includes both endpoints. Adjacent inclusive intervals can match the boundary event twice.

blocks.title: Before you run
blocks.body: Which city should receive the sale on exactly May 1?

code.source:
WITH dim(customer_id, city, valid_from, valid_to) AS (
 VALUES (42, 'Oslo', DATE '2026-01-01', DATE '2026-05-01'),
        (42, 'Bergen', DATE '2026-05-01', DATE '2026-09-01'),
        (42, 'Oslo', DATE '2026-09-01', DATE '9999-12-31')
), sales(customer_id, sold_at, amount) AS (
 VALUES (42, DATE '2026-04-20', 40), (42, DATE '2026-05-01', 60)
)
SELECT s.sold_at, d.city, s.amount FROM sales s JOIN dim d
 ON s.customer_id = d.customer_id
 AND s.sold_at >= d.valid_from AND s.sold_at < d.valid_to
ORDER BY s.sold_at;

steps.title: Point-in-time join

steps.title: Validate
steps.body: There should be no overlapping intervals for the same business key.
